Nature uses volcanic activity as a delivery system. Powerful eruptions push material from Earth’s mantle to the surface, carrying diamonds along the way. These eruptions happened millions of years ago, and they left behind extraordinary formations where diamonds are still found today. Those types of eruptions are, Kimberlite Pipes The primary source of gem-quality diamonds is kimberlite pipes. These are vertical, carrot-shaped structures formed by ancient volcanic eruptions. When miners search for diamonds, they often focus on these pipes because they are the wealthiest and most reliable sources. Some of the world’s biggest diamond mines, like those in South Africa and Botswana, come from kimberlite deposits. Lamproite Pipes Less common than kimberlites, lamproite pipes are another type of volcanic rock that can bring diamonds to the surface. While not as widespread, they are still important. For example, Australia’s famous Argyle Mine, which produced the world’s rare pink diamonds, was hosted in a lamproite pipe. passages.text: How Diamonds Are Created Deep Beneath the Earth’s Surface Share Diamonds are more than dazzling gemstones; they are the ultimate creation of Earth's raw and powerful forces. Formed far below the planet’s surface, they emerge from much intense conditions than a few other natural processes. Under unimaginable heat and crushing pressure, simple carbon atoms are transformed into one of the most complex and most coveted materials known to humankind. Unlike other minerals that form closer to the crust, diamonds begin their journey nearly 100 miles underground, in regions we can never directly reach. What makes them extraordinary is not only their physical brilliance but also their origin story, which stretches across billions of years and involves rare geological events. Understanding how diamonds come into being reveals both their scientific wonder and the reason behind their enduring value. In this blog, we will uncover the step-by-step journey of how Earth crafts these treasures beneath our feet. This unique process locks carbon atoms into a perfectly tight crystal lattice, giving diamonds their legendary strength. Why natural diamond formation is so unusual Carbon is common throughout Earth, and high pressures occur naturally deep underground. Yet natural diamonds are not found everywhere because their formation depends on several conditions occurring together. There must be an available source of carbon, a suitable pressure and temperature environment, and a chemical setting that permits diamond growth. The crystal must then survive its geological history, including any changes in temperature, pressure, and surrounding chemistry. Finally, the diamond must be transported close enough to the surface to be discovered. The volcanic systems that carry diamonds upward are relatively unusual, and many do not contain recoverable quantities of the mineral. passages.text: At their core, diamonds are composed entirely of carbon atoms, but what makes them extraordinary is how these atoms bond under extreme conditions. Deep within the Earth's mantle, carbon is subjected to intense pressure and heat that force it into a unique and tightly bonded crystalline structure, forming diamonds. Under these conditions, around 900°C to 1,300°C and pressures of 4.5 to 6 gigapascals (GPa), carbon atoms realign into a rigid tetrahedral lattice. This configuration is what gives diamonds their unmatched hardness and brilliance. In contrast, at surface-level pressures and temperatures, carbon prefers a different arrangement, forming graphite, so diamond's formation depends entirely on the planet's extreme underground environment. Where Diamonds Form in The Earth Diamonds originate deep within the Earth’s mantle, far below the surface where ordinary rocks and minerals are created. Geologists have determined that most natural diamonds form between 90 and 150 miles (150–240 kilometers) underground, where the balance of temperature, pressure, and carbon availability creates the perfect environment for their growth (Smithsonian Institution, Geology.com). At these depths, pressures reach more than 45,000 times greater than at sea level, and temperatures soar above 1,000°C. passages.text: Geological Timeframe of Diamond Formation Diamonds are not just beautiful gemstones; they are also among the oldest materials we can hold in our hands. Most natural diamonds began their journey 1 to 3 billion years ago, long before the first plants or animals appeared on Earth. This makes them older than the continents we live on today. The process is incredibly slow. Carbon atoms deep within the Earth’s crust were exposed to extreme heat and pressure for unimaginable periods, allowing them to bond into the rigid crystal structure we recognize as a diamond. Unlike many minerals that can form in a few days or years, diamonds require vast geological ages to reach stability. Because of this immense timescale, each diamond carries within it a story of Earth’s earliest history, an unbroken link to conditions that existed when our planet was still young. When we see a polished diamond today, we are not just looking at a gem; we are looking at a fragment of deep time, preserved in crystal form. How do Diamonds Travel To The Surface? The Role of Carbon in Diamond Creation Diamonds might look extraordinary, but at their core, they are made of something straightforward: carbon. This is the same element found in everyday things like pencil lead (graphite) and even in all living organisms. The difference lies in how the carbon atoms are arranged. Deep underground, when carbon is exposed to incredible heat and pressure, the atoms lock together in a tight crystal pattern. What’s fascinating is that carbon on the surface could never become a diamond; it needs the rare conditions found only deep within the Earth’s crust. That is why diamonds are so uncommon. How diamonds reach the Earth’s surface Ancient volcanoes are responsible for the final step in the diamond formation process. Magma surged from deep below ground, carrying diamonds along with it. As it cooled, it formed vertical, carrot-shaped pipes called kimberlites. These are the primary sources of the natural diamonds humans have ever recovered. Not all diamonds made it. Many remain trapped far beneath the surface, which means the gems humans have recovered represent a genuinely limited group. The last eruption of this kind happened around 20 million years ago. There won’t be another. Why the natural diamond formation process cannot be copied Natural diamond formation is a geological event, not an engineered one. This billion-year process happened deep within the Earth through heat, pressure and time on a scale that no laboratory can reproduce. While scientists can replicate the chemical and optical properties of natural diamonds, laboratory-grown diamonds (also known as synthetic diamonds, lab-created diamonds and LGDs) are produced in just a few weeks by one of two methods: High-Pressure, High-Temperature (HPHT) or Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD). Yes, diamonds typically form 90–150 miles beneath the Earth’s surface, deep in the mantle, where temperatures and pressures are extreme. How long does it take for diamonds to form? Yes, most natural diamonds took billions of years to develop. The slow crystallization under intense heat and pressure makes each diamond a tiny time capsule of Earth’s ancient history. Do all volcanoes bring diamonds to the surface? No, only certain types of volcanic eruptions, specifically kimberlite and lamproite pipes, can transport diamonds from deep within the mantle to the surface. Are lab-grown diamonds real? Yes, lab-grown diamonds are genuine diamonds with the same chemical and physical structure as natural ones. However, they form in a matter of months using technology like HPHT or CVD, rather than taking billions of years in Earth’s mantle.

passages.text: about Earth’s interior Diamonds are more than gemstones. They are natural records of environments that humans cannot directly observe. Because diamonds can preserve mineral inclusions and chemical signatures from their growth environments, scientists can use them to investigate the mantle’s composition and history. Some inclusions reveal the kinds of minerals present at depth, while the chemistry of a diamond may provide clues about the fluids or melts involved in its formation. Diamonds can also preserve evidence of ancient tectonic activity. If a diamond formed from carbon carried into the mantle by a subducting plate, its chemical characteristics may help establish a connection between surface processes and deep-Earth geology. Their ages can reveal when particular regions of the mantle experienced diamond-forming conditions. Comparing diamonds from different deposits can therefore help scientists reconstruct changes in the planet’s interior over geological time. Nevertheless, diamonds provide an incomplete record. They form only in certain environments, and the crystals that survive transport and are eventually discovered represent a small and selective sample of deep-Earth material. Their inclusions may also have been altered by later geological processes, making some histories difficult to interpret. passages.text: Home » Minerals » Diamond » How Do Diamonds Form? How Do Diamonds Form? Contrary to what many people believe, diamonds do not form from coal. Article by: Hobart M. King, PhD Table of Contents Methods of Diamond Formation Many people believe that diamonds are formed from the metamorphism of coal. That idea continues to be the "how diamonds form" story in many science classrooms. Coal has rarely - if ever - played a role in the formation of diamonds. In fact, most diamonds that have been dated are much older than Earth's first land plants - the source material of coal! That alone should be enough evidence to shut down the idea that Earth's diamond deposits were formed from coal. Another problem with the idea is that coal seams are sedimentary rocks that usually occur as horizontal or nearly horizontal rock units. However, the source rocks of diamonds are vertical pipes filled with igneous rocks. The carbon in natural diamonds comes from more than one source. Some originates in Earth’s mantle, where carbon has been present since early in the planet’s history or has been redistributed by geological processes. Other carbon may have originated at Earth’s surface before being carried deep underground. One important process is subduction. At a subduction zone, one tectonic plate sinks beneath another and descends into the mantle. Oceanic crust and the sediments deposited on it can contain carbon in minerals, organic matter, and carbonate rocks. As the descending plate heats up and undergoes chemical reactions, some of its carbon can be released into surrounding rocks and fluids. Under suitable conditions, this carbon may contribute to diamond formation. Some diamonds preserve evidence of carbon that was once part of surface environments, although the precise history varies from one deposit to another. Carbon can also circulate through the mantle in fluids and melts. These materials transport dissolved elements and compounds between rocks, allowing carbon to move from one geological setting to another. Changes in pressure,

How diamonds reach Earth’s surface Forming a diamond deep within the mantle is only part of its geological journey. To become accessible, it must travel upward without spending too long in conditions where it could transform into graphite or react with surrounding materials. Most economically important natural diamonds reach the surface through unusual volcanic eruptions involving kimberlite or, less commonly, lamproite. These rocks originate deep within Earth and can rise rapidly through the crust. Kimberlite magmas are rich in volatile components, including carbon dioxide and water, that help influence their behavior during ascent. As magma rises and pressure decreases, dissolved gases can expand, contributing to explosive volcanic activity. In some cases, this process excavates deep conduits through the surrounding rock. These conduits may form steep, carrot-shaped bodies known as pipes. When the magma cools and solidifies, it can preserve diamonds and other mantle minerals carried upward from depth. Our understanding of the origin of lithospheric diamond source fluids is better developed than it is for sublithospheric diamonds. This is because they contain much more nitrogen that can be studied along with carbon, and sometimes they are found still trapped within their peridotite or eclogite host rocks (figure 3). Since superdeep diamonds contain little or no nitrogen, and are never found within their original superdeep mantle host rocks, they provide less information about the geological conditions by which they formed. We do know, however, that the carbonate-rich fluids, metallic melts, and boron-rich fluids in superdeep diamonds all relate in some way to deeply subducted material from the earth’s oceanic lithosphere. But the challenge remains for geologists to predict where these domains, all with different oxidation states, occur in the deep earth.
